metaDescription: Six Tosima window cleaning robots compared, from the entry W2 to the W6 Pro, by suction, tank, nozzles, safety features and who each one suits.
expertTake: The Tosima X1 is the best balance in the range, with an 85 ml viewable tank and dual ultrasonic nozzles. The W2 is the value choice for plain jobs on small glass. If you have a large exterior or high-rise window, skip this brand's lineup and look at models that publish a rope length and backup battery duration.
introParagraphs: This brand sells a ladder of window robots whose names are barely descriptive, and the numbers do not always rise with capability. Two machines called W5 sit on different listings, and the W6 Pro is not simply a bigger W5.

The practical way through the range is to compare tank size, nozzle count, suction and the safety features each listing actually names. Six models are sorted here by those facts, with an honest note about where the listings stay vague.

products.name: Tosima X1 Dual-Nozzle Window Robot, 85 ml Tank
products.description:
The X1 is the Tosima that most clearly does what the others only describe. Its 85 ml tank is the largest in the range and has a window so you can read the level, which prevents the dry-pad surprise that mid-pane refills cause. Two ultrasonic nozzles atomise the water into mist that wets the cloth evenly.

The listing names a backup battery and a maximum-suction pump, though it does not give a runtime or a pascal figure, which is a gap worth noting. Against the W5, the X1 has a bigger tank but less detail on adaptive grip, so it fits owners who clean larger panes more than those who want the most documented grip system.

Wash the pads after each use, rinse the nozzles occasionally, and check that the tank cap seals fully. Use a rope on any window above waist height, since the listing offers no rope specification. Fill the tank only to the marked line and let the pad soak through for a few seconds before you set the robot on the glass, so the first pass does not skate over a dry cloth and leave dust trails behind.
products.bestFor: Everyday cleaning of medium to large panes with fewer refills.
pros: 85 ml tank is the largest in the range
Viewing window shows the water level
Dual ultrasonic nozzles wet the cloth evenly
Backup battery named in the listing
cons: No suction figure or backup runtime published
No rope specification in the listing

products.name: Tosima W5 Auto-Spray Window Robot, Triple Safety
products.description:
The W5 is the best documented grip system in the range. A variable-frequency pump moves between about 2400 and 3200Pa depending on what the robot senses on the glass, while the title advertises a 6400Pa maximum, so read the pair as a working range and a ceiling. Bidirectional ultrasonic spray wets the pad on both directions of travel.

The 65 ml tank is visible from outside, which is helpful, though smaller than the X1. A triple safety system is listed, which is a general statement. Compared with the WA9C Pro, the W5 has two nozzles instead of four but gives clearer information on suction behaviour, so it suits people who want predictability.

Keep the pads clean and swap them when the fibres mat. Wipe the suction seal before every run, use the rope on elevated panes, and note that the same name appears on two listings, so check the model you are ordering.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a clear explanation of how the grip behaves.
pros: Variable-frequency pump with a stated working range
Visible 65 ml tank
Bidirectional spray covers both directions
Triple safety system listed
cons: Two suction figures on one listing can mislead

products.name: Tosima WA9C Pro 4-Nozzle Window Robot, 6 Modes
products.description:
With four nozzles the WA9C Pro wets a pad more evenly than any two-nozzle sibling, and six cleaning modes give it the widest set of path choices in the range. Dirty or sticky glass benefits most, because even dampness is what loosens a film before the pad crosses it.

Its safety description includes power-failure protection, which is the feature that matters most for a mains-powered robot on glass. The listing does not publish a number for it, so treat it as a promise to verify at purchase. Against the X1, it has finer spray but a smaller stated tank, so on a big window it will need a refill sooner.

Rinse all four nozzles with clean water every few weeks, because more nozzles mean more places to block. Keep the cord clear and wash the pads after each job. When switching between its six modes, start with the one that matches your pane shape, because a top-down mode on a wide, short window wastes time on repeated turns, while a side-to-side pass finishes it in a fraction of the cycles.
products.bestFor: Sticky or dusty glass that needs evenly wetted cloths.
pros: Four nozzles wet the pad evenly
Six cleaning modes for different pane shapes
Power-failure protection in the safety list
Intelligent path planning
cons: More nozzles means more to clear of minerals

products.name: Tosima W6 Pro 7200Pa Window Robot With Storage Box
products.description:
The W6 Pro is the top of the stated suction range at 6400 to 7200Pa, and it comes with both an app and a remote so you can choose how to control it. A storage box in the package is a small but real convenience, since a window robot needs a clean, dry place that is not a cupboard floor.

That suction range is the highest published in this lineup, which helps on tall or awkward panes where a firmer seal builds confidence. The trade is that the listing says less about the spray system than the X1 or WA9C Pro, so check the tank size at purchase.

Store it in the box with the pads removed and dry. Check the seal ring for dust each time, and use the rope. If you rarely use the app, the remote alone is fine. Keep the box for the life of the robot, since it protects the pads and the suction ring from dust between seasons, and a robot that sits for months on a shelf is the one whose seal fails first.
products.bestFor: Owners who want the highest stated grip and a tidy storage solution.
pros: Highest stated suction range in the lineup
App and remote give two ways to control it
Storage box included
Bidirectional spray pattern
cons: Less spray detail than the X1 or WA9C Pro
Higher tier than the simpler models

products.name: Tosima W3 Dual-Direction Auto-Spray Window Robot
products.description:
The W3 is an earlier model that stays in the lineup for a simple reason: its feature set is stated plainly. A dual-direction auto-spray wets the pad as it moves, an anti-drop sensor and edge detection form part of a triple safety system, and the robot works out the size and shape of the window by itself.

It is a plain design with fewer modes than the WA9C Pro and a less detailed suction story than the W5, so it suits straightforward rectangular windows. Compared with the W2 it adds spray in both directions, which means better finish on the return pass.

Because it is an older model, check that spare pads and cloths are available, since a robot that outlives its pad supply quickly becomes a drawer item that nobody uses. Wash the pads after use, wipe the sensors that detect the edge, and use the rope on any pane above waist height.
products.bestFor: Simple rectangular windows at a modest tier.
pros: Dual-direction auto-spray wets on both passes
Anti-drop and edge detection form the safety set
Detects window size and shape
Plain design with few moving parts
cons: Older model with fewer cleaning modes

products.name: Tosima W2 3800Pa Window Robot, AI 3.0 Path Planning
products.description:
The W2 is the lowest-suction and lowest-tier Tosima here, with 3800Pa and AI 3.0 path planning, and it is the one to look at for a small flat. Microfibre pads, anti-fall sensors and edge detection cover the basics.

At this rating it is less suited to textured or very large glass, because less suction leaves less margin if the surface is dirty. Against the W3, the W2 leaves out the dual-direction spray, so expect a slightly less even finish on a dirty pane.

Keep the glass free of loose dust before you start, wash the pads each time and check the seal. Use the rope even on small windows, because a lighter robot still falls if the grip lets go. If a pane has a dark, deeply soiled patch, wipe that spot by hand first, because a low-suction robot that drags over a gritty smudge is more likely to lose its seal at exactly that point.
products.bestFor: Small windows and light dust in a flat on a tight budget.
pros: Lowest tier in the lineup
AI 3.0 path planning for ordered coverage
Anti-fall sensors and edge detection
Microfibre pads included
cons: 3800Pa gives the least margin on dirty glass

buyingCriteria.explanation: The names in this range do not rise with capability: the X1 has the biggest tank, the W6 Pro the highest suction range and the WA9C Pro the most nozzles. The W5 title lists 6400Pa while its description gives 2400 to 3200Pa. Choose by the specs you need, not by the number in the name.
A tank that runs dry means a dry pad smearing dust. The X1 has 85 ml and a viewing window, and the W5 has 65 ml with a visible gauge. For large panes, tank volume decides how often you pause.

The WA9C Pro has four nozzles, the X1 two, and the W3 sprays in two directions. More nozzles wet the pad more evenly, which loosens film before the pad passes. They also need more rinsing to avoid mineral blockage.

The W2 lists 3800Pa, the W5 2400 to 3200Pa working and 6400Pa maximum, and the W6 Pro 6400 to 7200Pa. A high ceiling matters less than a stable working grip. Ask which figure the robot holds in normal use.

Every model lists some form of triple safety, anti-drop or backup power, but few publish a runtime or rope length. The X1 names a backup battery and the WA9C Pro power-failure protection. Treat all of it as a starting point and use a rope.

The W6 Pro offers both app and remote, and most others rely on a remote or buttons. An app helps with progress but is not needed for a basic job. Pick the control you will actually use, and remember that a phone app also means a pairing step, an update now and then and a signal that must reach the window, which is not guaranteed in every room.

specDecoder.meaning: The pump speeds up and slows down with the surface, saving noise and wear. The listed range is the working grip.
specDecoder.watchFor: The W5 quotes 2400 to 3200Pa for this, which is lower than the 6400Pa in its title.

specDecoder.meaning: Water is broken into a fine mist that wets the cloth evenly. It is gentler and more even than a simple jet.
A routing method that covers the glass in ordered passes. The version number is branding, not a measurable quality.
A bundle that usually combines a backup battery, anti-drop sensing and a rope point. The parts matter more than the label.
specDecoder.watchFor: The W3 and W5 both use the phrase, so check what is inside.

specDecoder.meaning: How much water the robot carries per fill. A bigger tank covers more glass before a refill.
specDecoder.watchFor: X1 lists 85 ml and W5 65 ml.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stated specifications
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared only what each listing states, such as tank size, nozzle count and suction range. Where two figures conflict, as on the W5, we used the working range. Missing numbers counted against a model.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spray and tank design
howWeEvaluated.description: Tank volume and nozzle layout were weighed together, since they decide how evenly and how long the robot wets the glass. The X1's 85 ml and the WA9C Pro's four nozzles lead on different halves of that question.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety detail
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for named backup power, anti-drop sensing and power-failure protection. General phrases carried less weight than specific ones. No listing here publishes a rope length.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to the window
howWeEvaluated.description: Each model was matched to glass size and soil level, from the 3800Pa W2 on small panes to the W6 Pro on awkward ones. Owner feedback patterns on slipping and drying out supported the ordering.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across the range
howWeEvaluated.description: Relative tiers run from the W2 at the bottom to the W6 Pro at the top. A step up had to bring a larger tank, finer spray or a firmer grip, not just a higher name number.

rows: Highest suction range or best-documented grip

cards.label: Large tank
cards.text: The X1's 85 ml tank and viewing window mean fewer refills and no dry-pad surprises. It suits big panes and a calm cleaning session. It only has two nozzles.

cards.label: Many nozzles
cards.text: The WA9C Pro wets the pad evenly with four nozzles, which helps on film and sticky dust. It will need refilling sooner. It suits dirty but smaller panes.

howToChoose.note: Tank first for big glass, nozzles first for grimy glass.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A clear tank gauge, a simple remote and a safety list with named parts. Start on a ground-floor window so you can watch a full cycle. Read the listing for any claim you cannot verify.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The X1 is the easiest to read, and the W3 is the plainest to operate. The W2 costs the least and is fine for a few small panes.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your glass is large, tall or dirty. The X1, WA9C Pro and W6 Pro each spend money on tank, spray or grip.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a few small panes. The W2 or W3 will do.

maintenance.why: Trapped grit scratches glass and smears the finish. Dry them flat.
Minerals block fine nozzles, which the four-nozzle WA9C Pro is most prone to.

maintenance.task: Check the tank cap and seal
maintenance.why: A loose cap drips onto the glass and causes streaks.

maintenance.task: Wipe the suction ring and sensors
maintenance.why: Dust weakens grip and disturbs edge detection.
A damaged cord or rope removes the safety margin. Replace at the first sign of wear.

faq.a: The X1, thanks to its 85 ml viewable tank and dual ultrasonic nozzles. It covers medium and large panes with fewer refills, though it publishes no suction figure.

faq.q: Why do two Tosima W5 listings exist?
faq.a: The same name appears on different listings with different feature descriptions. Check the model details and the suction numbers before ordering.
A higher range means a firmer seal on awkward glass, but the rope and backup battery are what keep a robot from falling. Do not use suction alone to judge safety.

faq.q: Can I use these on exterior windows?
faq.a: Only with great care and a rope. None of these listings publishes a rope length or backup runtime, so check the building rules and use another model for high glass.
No. A remote is enough for basic cleaning. The W6 Pro offers both if you want progress on a phone.

faq.q: How often should pads be replaced?
faq.a: When fibres mat down or stop holding water, usually after a few months of regular use. Spare pads are inexpensive and worth keeping.
